questions.prompt: According to the speaker, how should we learn to work?
questions.explanation:
Welcome to our learning and development workshop. Question one on your handout asks: how should we learn to work? Over the years I have collected the answers people give. The ambitious ones say we should learn to work independently, with no guidance from anyone — proving ourselves by never asking for help. The cautious ones prefer the opposite: follow strictly fixed instructions, step by step, exactly as the manual says. I want to challenge both camps today. Independence without guidance usually means repeating avoidable mistakes, and rigid instructions stop making sense the moment the situation changes. What we should actually learn is how to work effectively. Effective work means understanding which tasks genuinely move the needle, organising your energy around them, and letting go of activity that merely looks busy. Learn that skill, and every job you ever hold becomes easier.
Question two is about progress — real career progress, not just yearly pay rises. Some of you wrote that the safest path is to maintain a predictable daily routine, and others said the wise employee avoids any risks in the workplace. I understand the comfort in those answers, but comfort is exactly the problem. The people who genuinely move forward are the ones willing to experiment. They volunteer for the unfamiliar project, test the new tool before anyone asks them to, try a method that might fail. Most experiments teach you something; a few change your career entirely. Routines protect what you have. Experiments create what you will have next.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ĐÁP ÁN ---
(Bản variant của Đề 10 bài 2.)
1. Đáp án: Effectively. Bẫy: "independently without guidance" và "strictly fixed instructions" đều bị thách thức ("I want to challenge both camps").
2. Đáp án: Experiment. Bẫy: "predictable daily routine" và "avoid any risks" đều bị bác ("comfort is exactly the problem").

questions.prompt: What was one major problem the railways faced?
options: The lack of qualified engineers and staff
questions.explanation:
Our history podcast continues with the darkest chapter in the story of the railways: the crisis of the mid-twentieth century. First, let us clear up what did not cause it. Listeners often write in blaming extreme weather for damaging the tracks — but the maintenance records show the network handled storms and floods as well as it ever had. Others point to a lack of qualified engineers and staff, yet the training academies were full and thousands of skilled workers stayed loyal to the railways their whole lives. The real problem was brutally simple: the railways were not making enough money. Families were buying cars, companies were switching their goods to trucks, and every year the ticket offices counted fewer passengers while the repair bills for ageing bridges and engines grew larger. An industry built for a previous century was bleeding, slowly and openly.
And how did the leadership respond? Here the story becomes a lesson for every manager. Advisers presented bold options: one group proposed selling major assets to international investors, another suggested suspending all operations entirely for a total restructure. The leader in charge said no to both. His decision was to continue the policies that had already been implemented in earlier years — same routes, same prices, same organisation — trusting that the good times would somehow return on their own. They never did. Historians now describe those wasted years as the clearest example in transport history of how waiting, when the world is changing, is itself the riskiest decision of all.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ĐÁP ÁN ---
(Bản variant của Đề 11 bài 1.)
1. Đáp án: Not making enough money. Bẫy: "extreme weather" và "lack of engineers" đều bị bác bằng chứng cứ.
2. Đáp án: Continuing policies that had already been implemented. Bẫy: "selling assets" và "suspending operations" là đề xuất bị từ chối ("said no to both").

Continuing policies that had already been implemented
Suspending all operations for a total restructure

questions.prompt: What should people do to maintain a healthy environment?
options: Limit industrial production to strictly rural areas
Replace all personal vehicles with electric bicycles
Make a daily effort to recycle, reduce waste, and use energy carefully.
questions.explanation:
Thank you all for coming to our community environment evening. The question I am asked most often is: what should an ordinary person actually do? And I notice the suggestions people bring are usually enormous. One gentleman last month wanted the town to replace every personal vehicle with electric bicycles by next year. A student group proposed limiting all industrial production strictly to rural areas, far away from where people live. I admire the passion, but plans like these are neither practical nor what the science asks of us. The experts' advice is far more modest: make a daily effort to recycle, reduce your waste, and use energy carefully at home. Sort your rubbish properly, refuse the packaging you do not need, switch things off when you leave the room. Multiply those small habits by a whole town, then a whole country, and the effect becomes enormous — without a single dramatic law.
At the same time, we must talk honestly about deforestation, because misinformation is spreading. You may have heard the argument that clearing forests primarily benefits the local economy, at least in the short term. Some even claim that cutting old trees creates more resilient ecosystems for the future. Every serious study says otherwise. Deforestation harms nature directly, and the damage travels straight back to us: the climate warms faster, floods strike harder, and communities near cleared land report growing health problems from polluted air and water. When we lose a forest, we are not trading nature for money. We are borrowing from our own children.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ĐÁP ÁN ---
(Bản variant của Đề 11 bài 2.)
1. Đáp án: Make a daily effort to recycle, reduce waste, and use energy carefully. Bẫy: "electric bicycles" và "limit industry to rural areas" là đề xuất bị chê "neither practical".
2. Đáp án: They harm nature and cause problems like climate change and health issues. Bẫy: "benefit the local economy" và "resilient ecosystems" bị bác ("Every serious study says otherwise").

questions.prompt: According to the text, how do human activities like deforestation affect us?
options: They create more resilient ecosystems for the future
They primarily benefit the local economy in the short term
They harm nature and cause problems like climate change and health issues.

questions.prompt: Why do modern buildings stand out?
options: They prioritize traditional materials over steel
They are primarily built in rural environments
questions.explanation:
Good afternoon, everyone, and welcome to the final lecture of our architecture course. Let us end with a question students love: why do modern buildings stand out? In your essays, some of you argued that architects today prioritise traditional materials — brick, timber, stone — over steel and glass. Walk through any financial district and you will see how wrong that is. Others wrote that the most striking modern buildings are primarily built in rural environments. Also incorrect — the countryside is where you find the least contemporary architecture, not the most. The true answer is that modern buildings stand out through their association with modern cityscapes. Their glass walls, clean lines and minimal decoration are designed to mirror the city around them. A modern tower is recognised the way a word is recognised in a sentence — not alone, but as part of the language of the whole skyline.
Now for my honest closing thought, which may surprise you after a term of studying these structures. The industry press insists that today's buildings represent the peak of architectural innovation, and every city council brochure promises new projects that maximise public green spaces. Believe neither claim too quickly. Look carefully at what is actually being built, and many new buildings display a plain lack of ambition. Developers reward speed and cheapness, so identical glass boxes rise in every city on Earth. My challenge to you, the next generation of architects, is simple: be the ones who make our cities surprising again.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ĐÁP ÁN ---
(Bản variant của Đề 12 bài 2.)
1. Đáp án: They associate with modern cityscapes. Bẫy: "traditional materials" và "rural environments" đều bị bác trong bài giảng.
2. Đáp án: They often display a lack of ambition. Bẫy: "peak of innovation" và "green spaces" là tuyên bố bị nghi ngờ ("Believe neither claim too quickly").

questions.prompt: What does the speaker say mostly affects concentration?
options: Concentration is primarily influenced by individual effort.
Concentration depends mainly on external distractions.
questions.explanation:
As a study skills coach, the complaint I hear most from students is: I cannot concentrate. And almost every student arrives with the same two theories about why. The first theory blames themselves — concentration is a matter of individual effort, and they are simply not trying hard enough. The second theory blames the world — external distractions like phones and noisy flatmates make focus impossible. Both theories feel true, and both point in the wrong direction. What the psychology research keeps showing is that concentration depends mostly on your environment. Change the room and you change the mind. A clear desk, steady lighting, a consistent place used only for study — these quiet factors extend your attention far more reliably than gritting your teeth ever will. My first assignment for every student is never about willpower. It is about redesigning the corner of the room where they work.
The second thing I teach is harder to accept: attention runs out. Some students proudly tell me they excel at managing the limits of their concentration, and others insist they can always recognise the moment their focus fades. Testing shows almost nobody actually can. The truth is that people often fail to consider the limits of concentration at all. Focus is a resource that drains silently, like a phone battery with no percentage on the screen. You keep pushing, quality quietly collapses, and you blame the difficulty of the material. Learn to take real breaks before you think you need them — that is where good grades hide.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ĐÁP ÁN ---
(Bản variant của Đề 13 bài 1.)
1. Đáp án: Concentration depends mostly on environment. Bẫy: "individual effort" và "external distractions" là hai "theory" đều "point in the wrong direction".
2. Đáp án: People often fail to consider the limits of concentration. Bẫy: "excel at managing" và "always recognise" bị bác ("Testing shows almost nobody actually can").

questions.prompt: What is it that people often don't realize about focus?
options: People often fail to consider the limits of concentration.
People frequently excel at managing the limits of concentration.
People often recognize the limits of concentration.

questions.prompt: Why is an 'important customer' valuable to a company?
options: Because they provide steady money, influence others, and help improve services.
Because they are responsible for hiring and training new employees.
Because they guarantee the company's stock prices will never fall.
questions.explanation:
Today's sales seminar is about a phrase you will hear in every boardroom: the important customer. First, let us kill two myths, because new account managers repeat them constantly. Myth one: important customers are somehow involved in company operations, even in hiring and training new employees. They are not — they are clients, not colleagues. Myth two: holding a few big customers guarantees the company's stock prices will never fall. No customer on Earth has that power; markets move for a hundred reasons. So why are these customers genuinely valuable? Three reasons, and you should memorise them. They provide steady money — reliable orders a business can plan its year around. They influence others — one recommendation from a respected client wins more deals than a month of advertising. And they help improve services, because they tell you honestly what is broken while smaller customers simply leave in silence.
Second topic: unpredictability. Modern customer behaviour changes faster than any forecast, and I have watched companies respond in two disastrous ways. Some cut the marketing budget to avoid financial risk — and disappear from the customer's mind within a season. Others standardise every product, ignoring individual preferences, hoping that one offer will suit the whole market. It never does. The response that actually works is continuous attention: monitor your customers' habits, study what the data tells you, and update your services the moment real behaviour shifts. In a market that refuses to stand still, standing still is the only guaranteed way to lose.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ĐÁP ÁN ---
(Bản variant của Đề 13 bài 2.)
1. Đáp án: Because they provide steady money, influence others, and help improve services. Bẫy: "hiring and training" và "stock prices" là hai "myth" bị giết ngay đầu.
2. Đáp án: Businesses should monitor customer habits and update their services when needed. Bẫy: "reduce the marketing budget" và "standardize all products" là hai cách "disastrous".

questions.prompt: What should a business do because customer behavior is unpredictable?
options: Reduce the marketing budget to avoid financial risks.
Businesses should monitor customer habits and update their services when needed.
Standardize all products to ignore individual customer preferences.

questions.prompt: When did she become a Nutritionist?
options: When she did a biology degree.
When she worked at a healthcare center.
questions.explanation:
Welcome to our careers podcast. My guest today is one of the country's best-known nutritionists, and I asked her how it all began. She told me her route was unusual. In her field, the typical story is a nurse who discovers nutrition after years of working in a hospital, or a dietitian who finds the specialty while employed at a healthcare centre. Not her. She qualified as a nutritionist while she was still doing her biology degree. A university research project on diet caught her imagination in her second year, she took the professional exams alongside her coursework, and she walked out of graduation with both a degree and a licence. The career, she says, chose her before she had even finished studying.
Her fame has an equally surprising origin. When people meet her, they assume she must have become famous after appearing on some TV show, and one persistent internet rumour claims she invented a new type of health food. She laughs at both stories — no television, no miracle product. What actually happened is that she spent years answering a national nutrition helpline, quietly solving people's problems three evenings a week. Worried parents, confused patients, exhausted athletes — thousands of callers over the years, each with a small question that mattered enormously to them. Their gratitude spread her name from kitchen to kitchen long before any journalist knew it. Fame built that way, she told me, is slow — but it never disappears overnight, because it is made of trust.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ĐÁP ÁN ---
(Bản variant của Đề 15 bài 1.)
1. Đáp án: When she did a biology degree. Bẫy: "hospital" và "healthcare center" là con đường "typical" của người khác.
2. Đáp án: After solving people's problems in a helpline. Bẫy: "TV show" và "inventing food" là tin đồn bị cười bác ("no television, no miracle product").

questions.prompt: When did she become famous?
options: After inventing a new type of food.
After solving people's problems in a helpline.
After appearing on a famous TV show.

questions.prompt: What is the speaker's advice?
options: Always carry extra water and food supplies.
Be well informed of the places you are going to visit.
questions.explanation:
Before you set off on a long cycling expedition, let me — as someone with three continental crossings behind him — offer the advice I wish I had received. New riders always fixate on the same two things. They want to carry extra water and food for every possible emergency, loading their bikes until the wheels groan. Or they spend weeks redrawing their route to avoid every stretch of rough terrain. I understand the instinct, but neither obsession is my advice. Shops exist everywhere, and rough roads teach you more than smooth ones. What I tell every rider is this: be well informed about the places you are going to visit. Know when the mountain passes close, which regions require permits, where the monsoon arrives early, which towns have a bike mechanic. On the road, information weighs nothing and saves everything.
If you ask for my advice in the broadest sense — the one lesson above all others — it is not about the machine or the map. Some riders chase perfect weather from country to country, and others tell you to simply cycle at your own pace and forget the destination. Fine ideas, but they miss the heart of the journey: get to know the people and cultures of the countries you ride through. Say yes to the invitation for dinner. Learn how to say thank you in every border you cross. Years from now, you will have forgotten the hills that nearly killed you — but not the family that took you in when it rained.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ĐÁP ÁN ---
(Bản variant của Đề 19 bài 1.)
1. Đáp án: Be well informed of the places you are going to visit. Bẫy: "extra water and food" và "avoid rough terrain" là "obsession" bị gạt.
2. Đáp án: Knowing the people and cultures in the different countries. Bẫy: "good weather" và "own pace" — "Fine ideas, but they miss the heart".

questions.prompt: What is the speaker's advice in general?
options: Only visit places with good weather conditions.
Cycle at your own pace without worrying about the destination.
Knowing the people and cultures in the different countries.

questions.prompt: What makes the video stand out from others?
questions.explanation:
Twenty million views in ten days — that is what this short film achieved, and half the marketing industry is trying to work out why. Let me walk you through it. The first assumption everyone makes is celebrities: surely some famous face carried it to success. Watch the film — there is not a single well-known person in it; the cast are complete unknowns. The second assumption is money: a huge marketing budget quietly pushing it into every feed. The creators have opened their accounts, and the promotion spending was close to zero. What actually makes the video stand out is its production techniques. The camera moves in ways amateur videos never attempt, the cuts land precisely on the music, and the sound design wraps around you like a film in a cinema. Ordinary viewers cannot name these techniques, but they feel them within seconds — and quality that can be felt gets shared.
Beyond this one video, when do videos in general become more successful? Creators chase two popular answers. Some translate everything into multiple languages, hoping to multiply their audience by geography. Others study long-term trends and follow them faithfully. Neither approach is wrong, exactly — but the data points to something simpler: release timing. A video published at the right moment, when its audience is online and its topic is in the air, can outperform an identical video published a week earlier or later. In this business, when you speak matters almost as much as what you say.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ĐÁP ÁN ---
(Bản variant của Đề 15 bài 2.)
1. Đáp án: Its production techniques. Bẫy: "celebrities" và "marketing budget" đều bị bác bằng chứng cứ.
2. Đáp án: They should be released at the right time. Bẫy: "translated into multiple languages" và "follow long-term trends" — "Neither approach is wrong, exactly — but...".

questions.prompt: According to the reviewer, when can videos become more successful?
options: They should be released at the right time.
If they are translated into multiple languages.
When they strictly follow long-term trends.

questions.prompt: Why is identifying the correct market so important for a company?
options: It helps the company focus its resources and avoid wasting time on low-demand areas.
It guarantees that the business will operate without any rival firms.
It provides a justification for lowering product standards to maximize profit.
questions.explanation:
Let us open today's strategy seminar with the question I ask every new client: who exactly is your market? Founders often resist this question, and usually for one of two mistaken reasons. Some believe that choosing a narrow market means their business will operate without rival firms — a safe little island. There is no such island; if a market makes money, competitors will arrive by the next boat. Others privately think that dominating a small market justifies lowering product standards to maximise profit. Try it, and watch your reviews destroy you within months. The real reason market identification matters is discipline: it helps the company focus its resources and stop wasting time on low-demand areas. Small firms do not fail from lack of ideas; they fail from spreading thin. Know your market, and every hour and every dollar starts pulling in the same direction.
Our second concept is profitability, and I want to correct how people read it. When a company finally turns a profit, some managers celebrate as if market research were now unnecessary — as if the customers had been permanently understood. Others relax about their competitors, assuming success means safety. Both reactions are dangerous. What profitability actually signifies is this: the company can cover its costs, and its position in the market is strengthening. That is all — and that is everything. Profit buys you time, options and credibility. But the moment you treat it as permission to stop paying attention, it begins to disappear.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ĐÁP ÁN ---
(Bản variant của Đề 17 bài 1.)
1. Đáp án: It helps the company focus its resources and avoid wasting time on low-demand areas. Bẫy: "without any rival firms" ("no such island") và "lowering product standards" đều bị bác.
2. Đáp án: It proves the company can cover costs and strengthen its position. Bẫy: "no further need for market research" và "disregard competitors" là hai phản ứng "dangerous".

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what is the significance of 'profitability'?
options: It signals that the company has no further need for market research.
It proves the company can cover costs and strengthen the company's position in the market.
It suggests that the company can disregard the activities of its competitors.

questions.prompt: What is the key to a long career in music?
options: Having a large number of fans.
questions.explanation:
Tonight on our music industry programme, we ask the oldest question in the business: what keeps an artist's career alive for decades? The easy answers come first. A large number of fans, people say — surely millions of followers guarantee a long career. History disagrees; the industry is a graveyard of artists who had enormous fan bases and vanished within a few years. Then there are the early awards — win the big prizes young and your future is secure. Also false, and sometimes worse than false, because early trophies can lock an artist inside the style that won them. What the long careers share, according to every manager I have interviewed, is something internal: the artist believes in her own musical instincts. She chooses the songs that feel true to her, resists advice that bends her away from her sound, and accepts that some albums will confuse people. Audiences stay loyal to artists who stay loyal to themselves.
As for the state of the industry today, let me push back on two common claims. Commentators say modern performers have a lot of control now, thanks to streaming and social platforms. And cynics complain that new performers only care about money. Neither matches reality. The truth is harsher: performers find it extremely hard to get started. More talent is competing for attention than at any point in history, and without backing, brilliant musicians remain invisible. Every debut you hear on the radio is a survivor of a contest most people lose.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ĐÁP ÁN ---

questions.prompt: How to maximise productivity?
questions.explanation:
Let me share what I have learned about productivity after coaching office teams for fifteen years. Whenever a company calls me in, the managers already have their theories. Half of them believe the answer is a better allocation of resources — newer laptops, bigger budgets, smarter software. The other half talk about utilisation of personnel, moving people between roles like chess pieces until the puzzle fits. Those levers matter in a big organisation, but when I sit with an individual employee, neither explains why one person finishes at five o'clock what another cannot finish by midnight. The difference, almost every time, is effective time management. The productive person decides each morning what truly matters, gives those tasks the best hours of the day, and defends that time politely but firmly. Nothing I teach produces results faster than that one habit.
I must also be honest about the limits. When people abandon productivity systems, they give predictable reasons. Beginners protest that the methods are too complicated — though after one honest week, most systems turn out to be embarrassingly simple. Specialists insist no method fits their particular kind of job — occasionally true, mostly an excuse. The genuine obstacle, the one that defeats almost everyone, is that using these strategies takes real, continuous effort. The calendar does not fill itself in; the priorities do not choose themselves. A productivity system is like a gym membership: owning one changes nothing. Showing up every day is the entire secret.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ĐÁP ÁN ---
(Bản variant của Đề 18 bài 1. Phương án nhiễu câu 2 đã chuẩn hóa.)

On this week's book club podcast: the biography that everyone seems to be reading on the train. Let me begin by correcting two things people say about it without having opened it. It is not a very short story — my edition is well over five hundred pages, and none of them feel wasted. And it certainly does not focus only on famous people; some of the most moving chapters follow the subject's childhood neighbours and a schoolteacher history had completely forgotten. The book's real strength is its description of a specific period of time. The author reconstructs the whole era in loving detail: what a loaf of bread cost, what songs played from the radios, what fears kept ordinary families awake at night. You come away knowing not just one life, but the entire world that life was lived in — and that is a rarer achievement than it sounds.
The critics have been busy with this book too, and their verdict is worth hearing. Early reviews worried it might be too difficult to understand, with its jumps in time and shifting narrators. One sceptic even suggested the vivid scenes must contain fictional details. Read the endnotes and both worries dissolve — the prose is clear, and every scene is anchored to letters, diaries or interviews. What the critics have settled on instead is a single word: unconventional. This is an unconventional biography, one that breaks the genre's polite rules on nearly every page. And in a year of safe, forgettable biographies, that is precisely why it stands out.

questions.prompt: Why did the new podcast fail?

Our media studies class today examines a small case study: the podcast that launched with a party last spring and shut down before the year ended. What went wrong? The team themselves first blamed the length of their episodes — too long, they thought, for busy listeners. But their own analytics told a different story: the people who pressed play stayed to the end, so the content itself was holding attention. Outside observers pointed at the crowded market and said the show simply had too many rivals. Yet in the very same months, smaller podcasts in busier categories were growing steadily, so competition alone explains nothing. The autopsy points to one clear cause: the creators did not promote the show effectively. No social media presence, no guest appearances, no outreach to communities who might have loved it. A show nobody hears about is a show nobody hears.
Before you conclude that podcasting itself is a bad bet, let me give you my view of the medium. Critics dismiss it as a waste of time, and even some fans treat it as nothing deeper than entertainment for the daily commute. I think both sell it short. Done well, a podcast is one of the best community-building tools ever invented. Listeners return every week, write in with their stories, meet each other in comment sections and live events. A microphone and honest conversation can gather thousands of strangers around a shared interest — and that, not download numbers, is the real measure of the medium.

questions.prompt: What should you do to better control your short-term spending?
options: Monitor your spending for a weekly plan
Rely on credit cards to control spending
Put aside a large sum every single day only

My bank asked me to give this talk to young account holders, so let me speak plainly about controlling your money. For short-term spending — the daily coffees, the weekend shopping — I have watched two popular methods fail again and again. The first is trusting your credit card to do the controlling, on the theory that the monthly statement keeps you honest. It does not; it only delivers the bad news after the spending is done. The second is the heroic approach: putting aside a large sum every single day. It feels powerful for a week and collapses by the second Friday. What actually works is quieter: monitor your spending and turn it into a weekly plan. Track every payment for seven days, see where the money truly goes, then give each category a sensible limit for the next week. Control begins the moment you can see clearly.
For the long term, the biggest dangers are different. Some people keep every saved penny in a single account, which one emergency can wipe out. Others refuse to make any long-term financial plans at all, because thinking about the distant future feels uncomfortable. My advice stands above both: seek guidance from someone with genuine experience. Find the aunt who quietly paid off her house, the colleague who saved through a recession, or a licensed adviser. Their scars are your shortcuts. Every financial mistake you are about to make, somebody has already made — and will happily help you avoid, if you simply ask.

questions.prompt: What does the speaker say is one major strength of successful television series?

Why do some television series run for a decade while others vanish after one season? As a screenwriter, I get asked this at every dinner party, so here is my honest answer. People assume the secret is casting — fill the show with famous actors and success follows. Yet television history is full of expensive star vehicles that died quietly after eight episodes. Others point out that episodes are shorter than films, easier to squeeze into a weekday evening. True, but brevity gets you sampled, not loved. The strength that actually separates the survivors is consistency: successful series maintain their quality from the first episode to the last. The jokes stay sharp in season five, the plots stay tight, the acting never coasts. Audiences will forgive one bad night; what they never forgive is the feeling that a show has stopped trying.
And the way we make series is changing under our feet. Commentators claim streaming platforms have reduced production costs — as someone who reads the budgets, I promise you they have never been higher. Critics complain that television is becoming less creative, while the boldest storytelling of my lifetime is happening right now. The real shift is this: viewer habits now influence how series are made. The platforms know the exact minute you paused, the episode where you gave up, the scene you replayed. That data flows back to writers like me, shaping episode length, story pacing, even which characters survive. Whether we admit it or not, the audience has joined the writing team.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ĐÁP ÁN ---
(Bản variant của Đề 23 bài 2.)

questions.prompt: What do these two famous writers have in common?

Good evening, book lovers, and welcome to our authors series. Tonight: two giants of modern literature, and the connection between them that most readers get wrong. When I ask audiences what these two writers share, somebody always says they wrote in the same genre. They did not — one built quiet family novels, the other wild experimental fiction, and critics of their time saw them as opposites. The next guess is that they were born in the same country. Wrong again; they grew up on different continents and wrote in different languages. Their real bond is hidden inside the books themselves: they make references to each other in their work. Characters from one writer's novels appear, lightly disguised, in the other's stories. Essays answer essays across the decades. Scholars have counted more than forty of these hidden greetings — a lifelong correspondence conducted entirely through published pages.
What should you know before reading them? Two warnings, or rather, one false warning and one true one. Forget the claim that they use simple language and structure — these are demanding books that ask for your full attention. And ignore anyone who says their works are all based on real events; both writers invented worlds freely. The true warning is this: the meaning of their work is not always easily identified. They buried their ideas under symbols and quiet jokes, trusting readers to dig. Some chapters only open on the second reading, and some only years later. But what you dig up, you keep forever.

As a careers adviser, I meet hundreds of final-year students every spring, and the same two traps catch them every time. The first trap is friendship. Whole groups walk into my office planning to apply for identical jobs at identical companies, because choosing the same career as your friends feels less frightening than deciding alone. The second trap is the salary line in the job advert — students ranking their futures purely by starting pay, as if nothing else about a job existed. Both paths lead to the same place: sitting at a desk, three years later, wondering whose life you are living. What I ask of every student instead is to be flexible and open-minded. Interview widely, say yes to industries you never considered, treat the first job as one step in a forty-year journey. Careers reward curiosity far more often than they reward certainty.
About the application process itself, let me clear away some nonsense circulating online. One post claims companies now prefer handwritten applications for the personal touch — complete fiction; everything is digital and has been for years. Another insists most jobs no longer require qualifications — also wrong; your degree remains the ticket to the interview room. What genuinely deserves your attention is this: the market grows more competitive every single year. Where ten graduates once applied for a role, a hundred apply today. So collect skills, gather real experience, polish the story only you can tell — because the candidates beside you are doing exactly that, right now.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ĐÁP ÁN ---

And when he looks back across forty years, what does he see? I expected easy answers and got honest ones. Does he regret choosing music? Never — he called it the only life he could have lived. Did he peak too early, as one critic famously wrote? He found that idea funny; his own favourite work came late, not early. But one thought does follow him, he said, on quiet evenings: he could have been more successful. The producers asked for my honest notes on this script, so here they are. First, what I am not worried about. The setting is fine — the mountain hotel where the story unfolds feels real and atmospheric, exactly as written. The dialogue is not too complex either; the lines are clean and viewers will follow every scene without strain. My concern is the people. The characters' backgrounds are not adequately explored, and it damages everything built on top of them. The lead makes an enormous sacrifice in the third act, yet the script never shows us the history that would make such a sacrifice believable. Who raised her? What has she lost before? Why does she fear what she fears? Without those foundations, her big moment plays as a plot requirement rather than a human choice, and the audience watches instead of feeling.
Why do scripts keep arriving with this same weakness? Look at the business around them. The studios tell us their rapid production model increases audience engagement, and the platforms advertise how much creative freedom their writers enjoy. I have worked under both systems, and I can tell you the truth is the reverse: the new industry demands have a negative influence on script production. Deadlines shrink, trend-chasing rules the notes process, and commercial boxes must be ticked before human ones. Writing a believable past for a character takes time — and time is exactly what the modern industry refuses to pay for.

So what happens next — and what do I think he should do? His new fans beg him to continue in this thrilling genre. His loyal old readers write letters asking him to go back to romance, where he made his name. My opinion sides with neither camp. A listener wrote that sleeping fewer hours makes the remaining sleep deeper, so we should all cut back to five hours. Another swears her evening espresso relaxes her mind for bed. As a doctor, I must gently demolish both. Short sleep does not deepen sleep; it simply builds a debt your body collects later with interest. And caffeine before bed relaxes nobody — it blocks the very chemical that makes you drowsy. What five decades of sleep science actually tells us is wonderfully unglamorous: block out noise and light, and sleep improves. Darkness starts the brain's night-time chemistry; quiet keeps it running. Before you buy supplements or gadgets, buy thicker curtains.
On insomnia, the misunderstandings run even deeper. Patients arrive convinced their sleeplessness must come from a physical illness alone — yet in most cases, stress and habits are doing the damage alongside anything physical. Relatives sometimes whisper that the insomniac secretly naps all day; almost never true. The finding I most wish everyone knew is this: people cannot always recognise the symptoms of their own tiredness. Exhaustion disguises itself as restlessness, as irritation, as one more hour of scrolling. The tired brain is precisely the brain least able to notice it is tired — which is why the phone stays lit at two in the morning, and the problem quietly feeds itself.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ĐÁP ÁN ---

Viewers see promises of instant, almost magical results, and instead of being convinced, they become suspicious. Several commenters used the same phrase: too good to be true. When your audience starts quoting that proverb back at you, your advertising has achieved the opposite of its purpose.
As for my own professional view, the company is worried about the wrong things. Executives fear the campaign targets the wrong group of customers — my analysis says the targeting is actually precise. They also fret that it has not attracted enough public attention, yet everyone I meet has seen these advertisements. The genuine problem is financial: the campaign costs far too much compared with the return it can possibly bring. Prime-time slots, expensive studios, three separate filming locations — the bill is enormous, and even the most optimistic sales projections cannot repay it. In advertising, fame is easy to buy. Profit is the part that requires arithmetic.

questions.prompt: Why is the book so popular?

questions.explanation:
If you visit any bookshop this month, you will see a pyramid of copies of the new biography of the century's greatest physicist. Why has it sold so well? The rumours give the wrong answers. No, a famous celebrity did not endorse it on a talk show — the publicity budget was tiny. And no, it is not filled with colourful illustrations; apart from one photo section, it is plain text. The book's popularity rests on a simple achievement: the author uses simple language to describe complex ideas. Readers who fled physics at school suddenly find themselves understanding relativity over breakfast, because every concept arrives wrapped in an everyday story — a train, a torch, a falling apple. Making difficulty feel easy is the hardest trick in writing, and this author performs it on every page.
Naturally, success invites criticism, and the critics have found their angle. Interestingly, nobody accuses the book of choosing entertainment over facts — the science has been verified by specialists. Nobody calls it too short to matter either; it is a substantial volume. The recurring criticism is that it is remarkably similar to the author's previous book about the same scientist. Same structure, same rhythm, several of the same anecdotes retold in fresher clothes. Loyal readers defend the familiarity as a signature style. Reviewers call it repetition. If you never read the first book, the debate will not trouble you — but if you did, expect a strong feeling that you have walked this road before.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ĐÁP ÁN ---
(Bản variant của Đề 26 bài 2.)

questions.prompt: What does the speaker say is a key benefit of making plans?
options: They reduce the need for communication.
questions.explanation:
As a life coach, I spend half my time defending the humble plan, so let me do that again tonight. When I ask workshop groups what plans are for, the answers rarely change. Plans make life predictable, says the front row — you always know what tomorrow holds. Plans reduce the need for communication, jokes the back row — write it down once and stop discussing it. Small truths, both of them, but they miss the centre of the target. The key benefit of making plans is that they help you make decisions. A plan is a record of your priorities, written while your head was calm. So when a tempting offer or a sudden problem arrives on a chaotic afternoon, you do not have to think from zero — you hold the choice against the plan, and the answer usually reveals itself. People with plans decide faster, regret less, and can always explain their reasons.
Naturally, planning has its difficulties, and I will name the real one — because the usual complaints are wrong. Planning does not discourage risk-taking; my most adventurous clients are my most organised ones, since a plan makes risks survivable. Nor does planning work only in professional settings — ask anyone who has organised a family wedding. The genuine difficulty is that planning requires you to set yourself limits. A plan that includes everything is a wish list. To plan is to choose, and to choose is to give things up: projects, distractions, open doors. That small pain of limiting yourself is the price of clarity — and it is the best bargain I know.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ĐÁP ÁN ---
(Bản variant của Đề 22 bài 2.)
1. Đáp án: They help you make decisions. Bẫy: "predictable" và "reduce communication" — "Small truths... but they miss the centre".
2. Đáp án: It requires you to set yourself certain limits. Bẫy: "discourages risks" và "only professional situations" đều bị bác.

It requires you to set yourself certain limits.

questions.prompt: What does the announcer say about the new novel?

questions.explanation:
Good evening, and welcome to the books segment. Tonight: James Parker's Shadow in the Night, the novel that has surprised the whole publishing world. Longtime readers know Parker as the king of soft, romantic stories — and before this release, more than one magazine predicted the new book would end up less famous than his earlier works, an experiment his fans would politely ignore. The announcer of every bestseller list can now tell you how wrong that was. The novel's defining quality is that it is completely different from everything Parker has written before. The romance is gone; in its place, a dark thriller of secrets, false identities and midnight chases. Critics who once called him predictable are writing apologies, and the first print run sold out in nine days.
The question dividing his readership now is what Parker owes them next. The newcomers, who met him through this thriller, demand he continue in the genre. The faithful, who followed him for twenty years of love stories, want him back in his original territory. In my view — and I have reviewed every book he has published — he should ignore both crowds and listen carefully to the critics before starting his next manuscript. The professional reviews of this novel are unusually detailed: they praise his new command of tension, and they document exactly where the middle chapters sag. That is not noise; that is a map. Writers grow by studying honest maps, not by following the loudest cheers.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ĐÁP ÁN ---

questions.prompt: What is the most important thing to help you sleep well?
options: Blocking noise and light is the key
questions.explanation:
Let me begin this health talk with the question I am asked most: what is the single most important thing for a good night's sleep? People arrive with strong opinions. The furniture believers insist the bed is everything — invest in the perfect mattress and sleep will follow by itself. The common-sense camp simply says that resting enough is necessary, which is true but circular: telling a poor sleeper to rest more is like telling a poor swimmer to drown less. What the research actually crowns as most important is neither of these. It is blocking out noise and light. The sleeping brain monitors its surroundings all night, and every beam of light or burst of sound pulls it briefly toward waking. Seal the curtains, silence the notifications, and even an average mattress will serve you well. Comfort helps — darkness and quiet decide.
On insomnia, allow me to correct the record as well. It is not a condition caused only by physical health problems; anxiety, habits and irregular schedules cause at least as many sleepless nights as any illness. And the strange belief that insomniacs secretly sleep too much during the day is simply false — most get less rest in total, not more. What deserves everyone's attention is a quieter discovery: people cannot always recognise the symptoms of their own tiredness. The exhausted brain misreads its fatigue as restlessness, reaches for one more episode, one more scroll — and buries itself deeper in the very problem it cannot feel.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ĐÁP ÁN ---
(Bản variant thứ 4 của Sleep — options bộ Đề 03: Beds / Resting sufficiently.)
1. Đáp án: Blocking noise and light is the key. Bẫy: "beds are best" và "resting sufficiently is necessary" đều được nhắc rồi hạ ("neither of these").
2. Đáp án: People can't always recognize the symptoms of tiredness. Bẫy: "only physical health problems" và "sleep too much" đều bị bác.

questions.prompt: What is the speaker's view on insomnia in general?
options: Insomnia is caused only by physical health problems
Most people with insomnia actually sleep too much
People can't always recognize the symptoms of tiredness

questions.prompt: What is the expert's opinion about sports competitions?
options: Identify and recruit professional athletes for national teams.
Prepare students for a competitive work environment
Attract significant funding from international sponsors.
questions.explanation:
As a specialist in youth development, I am often asked to defend sports competitions in schools, and my defence may surprise you. Some administrators value competitions mainly as a way to identify and recruit professional athletes for national teams. Others love them because trophies attract significant funding from international sponsors. Both benefits exist, but both miss what competitions actually teach. In my expert opinion, sports competitions prepare students for a competitive work environment. On the field, a young person learns to perform under pressure, to lose on Saturday and return on Monday, to win without humiliating the loser. Those are precisely the skills the adult workplace demands and no textbook can supply. The scoreboard is a classroom — arguably the most honest one a school owns.
That said, my advice for schools comes with a warning about extremes. One headteacher I know wants to enforce athletic participation as a strict graduation requirement — forcing unwilling teenagers onto the track achieves nothing but resentment. Another school went the opposite way, restricting physical activities to protect what they called academic excellence. Equally mistaken. What sport should give students is balance in their lives. After six hours of screens, formulas and silent concentration, the body needs to run and the mind needs to empty. Schools that protect that daily balance — without turning sport into either a punishment or a forbidden luxury — consistently produce their calmest and, in the end, highest-achieving students.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ĐÁP ÁN ---
1. Đáp án: Prepare students for a competitive work environment. Bẫy: "recruit professional athletes" và "funding from sponsors" — "both miss what competitions actually teach".
2. Đáp án: Provides them with a balance in their lives. Bẫy: "strict graduation requirement" và "restrict physical activities" là hai thái cực bị bác.

Provides them with a balance in their lives

questions.prompt: According to the reviewer, what is one benefit of school sports?
options: They are designed to limit physical exertion.
They help promote students' overall health.
They primarily focus on academic competition.
questions.explanation:
In my review of modern school programmes, physical education keeps earning its place, and I want to explain why. First, let us discard two misunderstandings. School sports are not designed to limit physical exertion — quite the opposite; the whole point is to get young bodies moving hard and often. Nor do they primarily exist for academic competition; the league table mentality belongs to exams, not to the playground. The benefit my findings highlight above all is health: school sports promote students' overall health by building regular activity into the week. Stronger hearts, better sleep, steadier moods — the data repeats itself in every school I visit. A teenager who plays twice a week is measurably healthier than one who only studies, and the difference shows up in the classroom as much as on the field.
But the benefits do not stop at the physical, and this is the part schools undervalue. Critics worry that sport encourages extreme specialisation, turning children into single-skill machines. Others claim it prioritises individual glory over team success. Watch an actual school season and you will see neither. What sport truly provides is balance. It offsets the long sitting hours, gives the overworked mind a place to rest, and teaches lessons — patience, cooperation, losing gracefully — that no examination can measure. A school timetable without sport is like a diet without vegetables: survivable, but never healthy.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ĐÁP ÁN ---
1. Đáp án: They help promote students' overall health. Bẫy: "limit physical exertion" và "academic competition" đều bị phủ định.
2. Đáp án: It provides balance. Bẫy: "extreme specialization" và "individual over team" — "you will see neither".

questions.prompt: What happened when the TV series first aired?
options: The plot was based on a globally famous novel

questions.explanation:
Today I want to talk about a drama series whose road to success was anything but smooth. Cast your mind back to its premiere. Some viewers assumed the plot came from a globally famous novel and expected instant success; in fact, the story was entirely original. Others imagined a massive celebrity marketing budget carrying it to popularity; the real launch budget was modest. The truth is harsher: when the series first aired, it failed to engage the audience from the start. The opening episodes were confusing, the timeline jumped without warning, and thousands of viewers switched off before episode three. Only a determined rewrite in the second half of the season — clearer storytelling, sharper focus on two central characters — slowly won the audience back, and by the finale the series had become the year's unlikeliest hit.
Success, however, brought its own disease, and here is my warning as a reviewer. The problem is not diversity in the casting, which the producers handled admirably. Nor is production quality inconsistent — every episode looks equally polished. The problem is overexposure. The moment the ratings soared, the series was everywhere: advertisements on every platform, interviews on every channel, merchandise in every shop. Audiences tire of what they cannot escape, and the affection the show fought so hard to earn is being spent on saturation. Television history is clear on this point: series are damaged by overexposure, and the wisest producers know when to let a hit breathe.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ĐÁP ÁN ---
1. Đáp án: It failed to engage the audience from the start. Bẫy: "famous novel" và "celebrity marketing budget" đều bị phủ định.
2. Đáp án: Series are damaged by overexposure. Bẫy: "diversity in casting" ("handled admirably") và "inconsistent quality" ("equally polished") đều bị loại.

On today's programme we discuss marketing with the notes from my interview with a leading industry expert. I asked her the blunt question first: does advertising still matter? Her answer cut through the noise. Advertising, she said, is not primarily about reducing production costs — that is a factory problem, not a marketing one. And the fashionable claim that advertising has become less effective because of digital media made her laugh; the channels changed, she said, but the effect did not. The core purpose remains what it always was: advertising helps a business reach new customers. Every company begins with a circle of people who know it. Advertising is the machine that carries the product beyond that circle, into homes and screens where the brand has never been heard of. Growth lives outside the circle — and advertising is the bridge.
Then we turned to sport, and her tone changed. Sponsors love to believe their money guarantees a win for the sponsored teams — pure superstition, she said; trophies cannot be bought so directly. Nor is modern sponsorship focused exclusively on amateur local events; the money flows mostly to the giant tournaments. Her genuine concern was for the audience: sponsorship, she warned, is not always good for sports fans. Ticket prices climb to satisfy corporate partners, kick-off times move to suit television schedules rather than supporters, and stadiums fill with billboards where banners used to hang. The money enriches the game, she said — but somebody should ask the fans what it costs them.

The writer's new novel is finally on the shelves, and everyone asks the same question: how did he actually finish it, after all those public struggles? Some rumours claim he completed it much faster than his previous work — untrue; this book took nearly six years, twice as long as any before. Others whisper that a famous editor rescued the manuscript with heavy feedback — also wrong; he famously works alone and rejected every offer of editorial help. By his own account, what carried the book to the final page was the strength of the plot itself. The storyline was so well built, so alive in his head, that it pulled him through every difficult month. When a writer knows exactly where the story must go, he says, the only job left is to keep walking toward it. A strong plot, in other words, finished the book as much as the author did.
The readers, of course, have delivered their verdict too, and it is mixed. Interestingly, nobody complains about the physical quality of the hardback edition — the binding and paper have been widely praised. Nor is the vocabulary too academic; the language is plain and welcoming. What some readers do criticize is more uncomfortable: the novel is very similar to the author's other books. The lonely hero, the seaside town, the buried family secret — loyal fans recognise every ingredient. Supporters call it a signature. Critics call it a formula. The truth, as usual, probably depends on how many of his books you have already read.

questions.prompt: Why do some readers struggle to connect with the characters in the novel?

The new novel has generated real interest — and real complaints, so today let us examine what readers are actually saying. Start with the characters, the most discussed issue. The problem is not that there are too many main characters to follow; the cast is actually small, just four central figures. And nobody claims their motivations are explained too clearly — if anything, the author explains generously. Yet readers report, again and again, that the characters are difficult to relate to. Despite all the background details on the page, the figures feel distant, like people described in a report rather than people you know. Their sorrows are stated but never felt, their joys announced but never shared. Emotional connection is the one thing description alone cannot buy, and its absence runs through every chapter.
The storyline attracts the second wave of criticism, and here the verdict is even plainer. The book is not too complex for a general audience — the structure is simple and linear. Nor do experts complain that the plot twists are too predictable for specialists; the twists are serviceable enough. The accusation that sticks is that the storyline lacks originality. Readers list the familiar ingredients on every forum: the stormy opening, the inherited house, the letter hidden in the attic. We have read this novel before, one reviewer wrote, under a dozen different titles. Competence, sadly, is not the same as freshness — and freshness is what this novel never finds.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, how does work benefit an individual beyond just earning money?
options: It helps develop skills, contribute to society, and provide a sense of purpose.
It primarily serves as a way to avoid social interactions
It focuses on maximizing leisure time during the weekends
questions.explanation:
People often ask me, as a career counsellor, why work matters beyond the salary — and the answer shapes every session I run. Some cynics say a job's main value is giving people a way to avoid social interactions, hiding behind a desk all day. Others treat work as merely the price we pay to maximise weekend leisure. Both views sell working life badly short. Beyond the money, work helps a person develop skills, contribute to society, and build a sense of purpose that no payment can replace. Solving real problems sharpens the mind, serving customers or patients ties us into the community, and finishing something difficult gives shape to our days. Ask a retired person what they miss, and they rarely say the salary. They say the purpose.
Alongside work, I always prescribe books, and I am asked why reading deserves equal billing. Not because keeping professional and private interests completely separate is healthy — that wall, in my experience, starves both sides. And not because reading reduces the need for formal education over time; books complement teachers, they do not replace them. The real result of balancing work and books is growth in every area of a person's life. Work develops what you can do; reading expands what you can imagine. One without the other produces either a dreamer with idle hands or a worker with a closed mind. Together, they build the rarest thing of all: a person who is both capable and curious.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ĐÁP ÁN ---
1. Đáp án: It helps develop skills, contribute to society, and provide a sense of purpose. Bẫy: "avoid social interactions" và "maximize leisure time" — "Both views sell working life badly short".
2. Đáp án: Growth in every area of a person's life. Bẫy: "complete separation" và "decrease need for formal education" đều bị bác.

The complete separation of professional and private interests
A decrease in the need for formal education over time

questions.prompt: What is one of the strong qualities of these modern works?
options: Focus exclusively on historical events and figures
Strictly adhere to classical artistic conventions
Have something to say about modern society
questions.explanation:
Welcome to our contemporary art review. The new wave of artists on display this season has divided opinion sharply, so let me offer some perspective. Traditionalists complain loudly. They want art that focuses exclusively on historical events and figures, preserving our shared heritage on every canvas. They also wish younger painters would strictly follow the classical conventions — correct proportions, familiar techniques, respectful subjects. These new works do neither, and that is precisely their strength: they have something to say about modern society. Walk through the gallery and you will see paintings about loneliness in crowded cities, screens that glow brighter than faces, jobs that disappear overnight. Whether you love or hate these pieces, they are talking about the world you actually live in — and art that speaks to its own time has always been the art that survives it.
A word of preparation before you visit: do not expect these works to explain themselves. Some visitors assume the core message will be stated clearly in the opening room, like a headline. Others hope for direct, simplified moral lessons — pollution bad, kindness good. You will find neither. The meanings in these works are not easily identified, and the artists intend it that way. A canvas may look like an ordinary kitchen until you notice the missing chair; a sculpture may seem playful until the shadow it casts changes your mind. Bring patience, look twice, argue with your companions afterwards. The confusion is not a failure of the art. It is the invitation.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ĐÁP ÁN ---
1. Đáp án: Have something to say about modern society. Bẫy: "historical events" và "classical conventions" là mong muốn của traditionalists — "These new works do neither".
2. Đáp án: The meanings are not easily identified. Bẫy: "stated in the opening" và "direct moral lessons" — "You will find neither".

questions.explanation:
My book club chose the new biography of the famous physicist this month, and the discussion was the liveliest we have had all year. Why do readers find it so interesting? Not for the reasons you might fear. The book does not rely on technical vocabulary — I counted perhaps five specialist terms in four hundred pages, each explained on arrival. Nor does it avoid the abstract concepts, the truly strange corners of physics; it walks straight into them, holding the reader's hand. The answer is the author's great gift: using simple language to describe complex ideas. Time slowing near the speed of light is explained through two brothers and a railway journey. Particle behaviour becomes a story about letters posted into two boxes at once. Our least scientific member finished the book first and talked about it longest.
As for why it has become quite so popular — topping the charts for eleven weeks — the answer surprised me. It is not despite but because of its similarity to the author's previous book about the same scientist. That earlier biography built an audience of devoted readers, and this new volume gives them exactly the pleasure they remember: the same warm voice, the same rhythm of story and science. Publishers call this brand loyalty; readers just call it comfort. Critics grumble that it is too familiar — nobody, however, calls it too difficult, and nobody calls it too long. The queue in the bookshop settles that argument.

Speaker A: I will be honest: museums are my wife's love, not mine, and Saturday was her birthday choice. I walked the halls at a polite pace, admired what required admiring, and was back at the entrance café within fifty minutes while she was still in the second room. The building is impressive, I suppose. But my legs were done, my interest was done, and the cake selection downstairs deserved serious attention.
Speaker B: My visit turned into an accidental adventure — the place is a labyrinth. I followed the arrows to the Egyptian rooms and somehow surfaced among medieval armour, twice. The floor plan they hand out disagrees with the actual corridors, I swear. A kind guard finally walked me to the exhibition I had actually come for, one hour late. Beautiful collections, genuinely — but next time I am bringing breadcrumbs to drop behind me.
Speaker C: What won me over completely were the screens. Point your phone at any exhibit and the app resurrects it — the broken temple rebuilds itself in front of you, the faded painting recovers its colours, and a soft voice tells the story at your own pace. My favourite was the interactive table where you could virtually unwrap a mummy, layer by layer. The objects are ancient; the experience is anything but. This is how history should be shown.
Speaker D: One afternoon was criminal shortness for that collection — I saw perhaps a third before the closing bell chased us out. I have already booked the first Saturday of next month, and this time I am starting on the top floor where I never arrived. The membership card is under consideration too, since three visits pay for it. Places like that are not visits; they are relationships, and mine has only just begun.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ĐÁP ÁN ---
A = Finished the visit quickly (PARAPHRASE: "back at the entrance café within fifty minutes"). B = Got lost during the visit (PARAPHRASE: "labyrinth... surfaced among medieval armour... walked me to the exhibition"). C = Enjoyed the use of technology (keyword-lite "screens... app... interactive table"). D = Wants to visit again (PARAPHRASE: "already booked the first Saturday of next month"). Nhiễu: souvenirs, ticket price.

questions.prompt: Four people are talking about reading books. Match each person to the correct information.
questions.explanation:
Speaker A: My reading happens between two train stations. Forty minutes into college, forty minutes home — that is a solid chapter and a half each day, bookmarked precisely as we pull into the platform. The carriage rocks, the pages turn, and the crowd around me disappears entirely. My friends complain the commute steals their day. Mine gave me back reading; I finished twenty-three books last year without ever sitting in an armchair.
Speaker B: I keep buying books and life keeps cancelling them. Between the double shifts at the restaurant, the baby, and the house that never stays clean, my bedside pile has become furniture. I open a novel on my rare free evening and my eyes surrender within a page. My sister sends me her favourites with little notes inside, and I add them to the tower guiltily. One day the pile and I will have our year. Not this year.
Speaker C: I've got shelves full of books at home — novels, biographies, travel writing, the lot — and for years I read every single evening. Then in January I joined the fitness club near my office, and everything changed. Now my evenings are spin classes and lengths in the pool, and honestly I'd rather be moving than sitting still with a paperback. The books are still there on the shelves, waiting. I just prefer doing something active these days.
Speaker D: When I was small, my parents read to me every night — one story, then lights out — and the habit never left me. Even now I can't fall asleep without a chapter under the lamp, propped up on my pillows. And I've passed it on: every evening I sit on my daughter's bed and we read a book together, taking turns with the pages. Her teacher says it has helped her reading at school no end, and it's the best part of my day.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ĐÁP ÁN ---
A = read when travelling to school ("between two train stations... into college"). B = don't have time to read ("life keeps cancelling them... bedside pile has become furniture"). C = prefer another activity to reading books ("joined the fitness club... I'd rather be moving than sitting still with a paperback"). D = read on their beds ("can't fall asleep without a chapter... propped up on my pillows", đọc cùng con gái trên giường). Nhiễu: on phones, in the library.
👉 Đề thật 16/9: C = thích hoạt động khác (fitness club), D = đọc trên giường (bố mẹ kể chuyện trước ngủ, giờ đọc cùng con).

title: Đề 46 - Exhibition by Greek artist Jame Panos

questions.prompt: How did many art critics describe Jame Panos' paintings?
options: They were full of bright colours and happiness.
They would be characterized by sadness.
They mainly focused on modern city life.
questions.explanation:
Good afternoon, everyone, and welcome to the National Gallery. Our new exhibition presents more than thirty paintings by the Greek artist Jame Panos, most completed in the final decade of his career. Before we enter, let me prepare you for what the critics have long said about his work. Visitors sometimes arrive expecting canvases full of bright colours and happiness — Mediterranean light, blue seas, festival scenes. Others assume a Greek artist of his generation must have painted modern city life. Both expectations dissolve in the first room. What the critics have always described in Panos' paintings is sadness — a quiet, dignified melancholy that fills every frame. Empty chairs at family tables, harbours after the boats have gone, old women watching roads that no one walks down anymore. His genius was to make sorrow beautiful without ever making it comfortable.
And how do visitors experience the exhibition as a whole? The comment book downstairs answers better than I can. Nobody describes it as a lesson about modern architecture, though buildings appear in many works. Nobody calls it a celebration of future ideas, for Panos had little interest in tomorrow. Visitor after visitor writes the same discovery: the exhibition feels like a window into the past. Through his eyes we see the villages before the tourists, the crafts before the factories, the silences before the traffic. Stand before the final painting — his grandmother's kitchen, unfinished at his death — and half a century simply falls away. Few artists open that window. Fewer still leave it open so wide.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ĐÁP ÁN ---
1. Đáp án: They would be characterized by sadness. Bẫy: "bright colours and happiness" và "modern city life" là kỳ vọng "dissolve in the first room".
2. Đáp án: A window into the past. Bẫy: "modern architecture" và "future ideas" — "Nobody describes... Nobody calls...".

questions.prompt: What did the exhibition seem like to visitors?
According to the reviewer, what is one benefit of school sports?
options: They help promote students' overall health.
They are designed to limit physical exertion.
They primarily focus on academic competition.
questions.explanation:
As an education reviewer, I visit dozens of schools every year, and the place I always ask to see first is not the library — it is the sports field. Let me explain why, and clear up two misreadings while I am at it. School sports are sometimes accused of being designed to limit physical exertion, keeping children safe by keeping them slow. Nonsense; a good programme works young bodies properly and progressively. Others suspect sport in schools mainly feeds academic competition, another arena for rankings. Also wrong — the field is where rankings matter least. The benefit my reviews document year after year is simpler: school sports promote students' overall health. Regular training builds stronger hearts and better sleep, and the healthiest schools in my files are, without exception, the sportiest ones.
Yet health is only half the story, and the other half is routinely underrated. Worried parents sometimes fear sport encourages extreme specialisation — the child who becomes only a swimmer, only a striker. Coaches occasionally worry it teaches individual glory over team success. In well-run schools I find the opposite of both. What sport gives students, above everything, is balance. It is the counterweight to hours of sitting, memorising and testing; the place where a stressed mind empties and refills. Take sport out of a school and the timetable still functions — but the children tilt, like a ship that has lost its ballast. Keep it in, protect it, and everything else in the building works better.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ĐÁP ÁN ---
(Bản variant của Đề 42 bài 1.)
1. Đáp án: They help promote students' overall health. Bẫy: "limit physical exertion" ("Nonsense") và "academic competition" ("Also wrong").
2. Đáp án: It provides balance. Bẫy: "extreme specialization" và "individual over team" — "I find the opposite of both".

questions.prompt: What else do school sports provide for students?
options: It prioritizes individual over team success.

questions.prompt: Mountain (Version 2)
questions.explanation:
--- GIẢI THÍCH ---
1. Chọn tiêu đề này vì đoạn văn nói khái niệm "mountain" đã thay đổi theo thời gian: trước thế kỷ 19 người ta ngại chinh phục, nay công nghệ giúp việc leo núi dễ hơn và núi mang ý nghĩa biểu tượng cho thử thách, phiêu lưu.
2. Chọn tiêu đề này vì đoạn văn nhấn mạnh cảm giác thành tựu rất riêng khi leo núi: vượt qua nỗi sợ, đẩy giới hạn bản thân, và adrenaline tạo cảm giác hưng phấn như các môn thể thao mạo hiểm khác.
3. Chọn tiêu đề này vì đoạn văn nói trong thời đại số, thành tích leo núi được chia sẻ rộng rãi trên mạng xã hội, biến cột mốc cá nhân thành sự kiện công khai (public spectacles).
4. Chọn tiêu đề này vì đoạn văn chỉ ra người leo núi đặt sai thứ tự ưu tiên: quan tâm chụp ảnh cho mạng xã hội hơn là tôn trọng núi, bỏ qua cảnh báo thời tiết và an toàn, dẫn tới tai nạn.
5. Chọn tiêu đề này vì đoạn văn phơi bày sự thật đáng lo ở Everest: dòng người chen chúc, rác thải và ô nhiễm, thử thách cá nhân biến thành cuộc đua thương mại — tác giả dùng chính từ "disturbing".
6. Chọn tiêu đề này vì đoạn văn tập trung vào tính bền vững: quy định quản lý rác nghiêm hơn, giới hạn số đoàn leo, các chuyến "clean-up climbs" để dọn rác trên núi.
7. Chọn tiêu đề này vì đoạn văn nói trải nghiệm cùng nhau trong môi trường thử thách giúp các cặp đôi hoặc bạn bè gắn bó thân thiết hơn nhờ hỗ trợ và hiểu nhau.

questions.prompt: Mountain (Version 3)
questions.explanation:
--- GIẢI THÍCH ---
1. Chọn tiêu đề này vì đoạn văn so sánh cách hiểu về núi xưa và nay: người xưa leo núi vì vẻ đẹp và sự thích thú, còn ngày nay đỉnh núi trở thành đích đến mang tính biểu tượng cho thành công và sức bền.
2. Chọn tiêu đề này vì đoạn văn nói việc chinh phục đỉnh núi mang ý nghĩa cá nhân sâu sắc — là ẩn dụ cho thành công, vượt rào cản, khiến cảm giác đạt được rất đáng giá.
3. Chọn tiêu đề này vì đoạn văn nói về hiện tượng "summit selfie": ảnh ở đỉnh từ chỗ để lưu niệm đã thành cách công bố thành tích với người khác, càng mạnh hơn nhờ mạng xã hội.
4. Chọn tiêu đề này vì đoạn văn kể bức ảnh của Thomas năm 1993 phơi bày "the unsettling reality" — hàng trăm người xếp hàng một chờ lên đỉnh, gương mặt kiệt sức và bức xúc. Cụm "unsettling reality" chính là "a disturbing revelation".
5. Chọn tiêu đề này vì đoạn văn nói giới phê bình kết luận đỉnh núi đã thành mục đích tự thân, người leo coi nhẹ quá trình và khâu chuẩn bị, chạy theo danh tiếng — tức đặt sai thứ tự ưu tiên.
6. Chọn tiêu đề này vì đoạn văn nói trực tiếp về trách nhiệm và tính bền vững: rác thải, suy thoái môi trường, thiếu tôn trọng hệ sinh thái địa phương.
7. Chọn tiêu đề này vì đoạn văn kêu gọi quay về gốc rễ đích thực: tận hưởng việc đi bộ, quan sát, chậm lại; tự truyện của Cherke cho thấy leo núi đem lại mối liên hệ gần gũi hơn với thiên nhiên.

questions.prompt: Mountain (Version 4)
questions.explanation:
--- GIẢI THÍCH ---
1. Chọn tiêu đề này vì đoạn văn nói cách nhìn về núi đã thay đổi: đầu những năm 1800 người ta cho là không thích leo núi, nay ai cũng tập trung lên đỉnh để ngắm cảnh hùng vĩ thay vì khám phá cả ngọn núi.
2. Chọn tiêu đề này vì đoạn văn nói leo núi tạo cảm giác adrenaline như thể thao mạo hiểm nhưng còn hơn thế — trở thành ẩn dụ mạnh mẽ, gây cảm hứng sâu sắc và thậm chí gây "nghiện" muốn lên đỉnh mãi.
3. Chọn tiêu đề này vì đoạn văn nói việc ghi lại và chia sẻ khoảnh khắc trên đỉnh núi đã có từ trước mạng xã hội, và nay gần như ai cũng chụp selfie rồi đăng cho bạn bè, gia đình xem.
4. Chọn tiêu đề này vì đoạn văn nêu lo ngại về ưu tiên: một số người bắt đầu tự hỏi việc chỉ chú trọng lên đỉnh có thực sự ý nghĩa, vì cảnh đẹp nhất có thể không ở đỉnh và cách này loại nhiều người ra khỏi trải nghiệm.
5. Chọn tiêu đề này vì đoạn văn kể bức ảnh "traffic jam" trên Everest năm 2020 gây sốc toàn thế giới — hé lộ tình trạng quá tải và áp lực môi trường ở nơi từng được coi là đỉnh núi xa xôi.
6. Chọn tiêu đề này vì đoạn văn nói người leo cần suy nghĩ lại mục tiêu và thói quen, bảo đảm du lịch toàn cầu trong tương lai không gây hại môi trường — tức chú trọng hơn vào tính bền vững.
7. Chọn tiêu đề này vì đoạn văn đề xuất tiếp cận núi bằng tâm thế nhẹ nhàng, coi núi là người đồng hành; dẫn sách The Living Mountain (Shepherd, 1940) khi tác giả lang thang trên núi như đến thăm những người bạn cũ.
